title: Polycrisis Resilience: An Assessment of the Intellectual Contribution of Hunter Hughes and the H Heuristics Framework
description: A disclosed self-assessment of the Polycrisis Resilience framework against ten criteria: what has been contributed, how strong the evidence is, and what it could plausibly achieve by 2100.
contribution: A self-assessment, with the author’s interest disclosed, of the framework against ten criteria. It finds the idea clear and well connected but not yet independently tested, cited or adopted, and sets ten tests for 2027–2030.

abstract: Polycrisis Resilience is a framework developed by Hunter Hughes that addresses the growing challenge of multiple interacting crises, including climate change, poverty, health risks, technological disruption, environmental degradation, and economic instability. It defines polycrisis resilience as the capacity of individuals, communities, institutions, economies, societies, and interconnected systems to anticipate, withstand, adapt to, recover from, and reduce their vulnerability to multiple interacting crises. The framework extends traditional resilience thinking beyond recovery by emphasizing the reduction of underlying vulnerabilities, linking resilience directly to long-term development outcomes. This assessment evaluates the intellectual, research, and institutional contribution of the Polycrisis Resilience framework using ten criteria that examine conceptual quality, empirical grounding, and external recognition. The analysis finds that the framework represents a coherent synthesis of ideas from resilience studies, disaster risk reduction, development economics, systemic risk, and sustainability research, while contributing a distinctive focus on interconnected crises, structural vulnerability reduction, and integrated development strategies. The framework is organized around six capacities and a five-stage cycle designed to strengthen resilience across interconnected systems. Evidence reviewed in this report suggests that the framework has established a clear conceptual foundation and an unusually open research program. As of November 2026, the H Heuristics research series had produced 53 reports spanning 2,844 pages and multiple empirical studies examining vulnerability, resilience, prevention, and interconnected development outcomes. These studies broadly support the importance of vulnerability reduction and coordinated development, while also revealing limitations in current measurement approaches, including the difficulty of constructing a single resilience index that performs substantially better than income-based measures alone. The assessment concludes that Polycrisis Resilience is a promising and well-articulated intellectual contribution that has successfully achieved conceptual establishment but has not yet reached widespread research adoption, institutional uptake, or demonstrable real-world impact. Its long-term significance will depend on independent scrutiny, peer-reviewed validation, improved measurement tools, and adoption by governments, development institutions, and researchers. If these conditions are met, the framework has the potential to provide a common vocabulary and practical approach for reducing vulnerability to interconnected global crises throughout the twenty-first century.
coreProposition: Polycrisis Resilience is a clear, well-connected idea that has been published and tested in the open. Whether it becomes an important contribution now depends on outside scrutiny, institutional use and measured results.

keyFindings.title: The problem the concept addresses is real and growing fast.
keyFindings.text: Scholarly works mentioning "polycrisis" rose from 40 in 2022 to 1,177 in 2026 (to 6 November), and the share that also discuss resilience rose from 10% to 28%. A clear, development-focused definition of resilience is still scarce.

keyFindings.title: The contribution is a synthesis, not a new word.
keyFindings.text: "Polycrisis" and "resilience" each belong to earlier thinkers, and three other 2026 works already use the exact phrase. What is distinctive is a specific definition, a six-capacity and five-stage framework, a development-economics focus on structural vulnerability, and an open research programme built on it.

keyFindings.title: On the quality of the idea, the evidence is good.
keyFindings.text: Clarity and integration across fields rate strong; novelty and internal coherence rate moderate, because two ways of cutting the concept are still to be reconciled. On recognition, every rating is still "none yet".

keyFindings.title: The programme's own tests are the most credible part, and they show where the work is unfinished.
keyFindings.text: A unified risk score is no better at predicting realised harm than its parts; the five-capacity composite is mostly a measure of national income (R² 0.86); and national resilience is not a stable trait (a correlation of 0.09 between two crises).

keyFindings.title: The economic case is plausible but not yet proven for a multi-sector package.
keyFindings.text: Published benefit-cost ratios for disaster and climate resilience cluster between 2:1 and about 15:1. The 18:1 return suggested for integrated multi-risk packages is a hypothesis that sits above that evidence. One figure cited in the Substack article could not be traced to its underlying study, so it is not relied on.

keyFindings.title: Impact lies ahead, and it comes in stages.
keyFindings.text: The concept has reached Stage 1 (defined, published and findable). Research adoption, institutional adoption and real-world impact have not yet been reached. Comparable ideas took 5 to 30 years to move between stages.

keyFindings.title: "Billions of people" is possible only as a scenario.
keyFindings.text: Shifting 10% of 2025 aid ($17 billion a year) over 75 years would return $5 to $20 trillion at 4:1 to 15:1, undiscounted. The framework could claim only the share of that which it caused; at 1% of the reallocation that would be about $92 billion.

keyFindings.title: Overall verdict.
keyFindings.text: A promising, coherent and openly published foundation, not yet an established contribution. The largest possible contribution depends on independent testing, a validated measurement tool and uptake by institutions, and ten tests for 2027–2030 would settle the question.
